reason: The provided sources do not support the topic's core premise that Andromeda's hot gas halo touches the Milky Way; only S1 mentions a gas halo (stating it extends only halfway), and no second source corroborates it.
story: Located approximately 2.5 million light-years away, the Andromeda Galaxy is the closest major galactic neighbor to our Milky Way. But Andromeda is not keeping its distance. Precise tracking shows Andromeda is hurtling toward us at roughly 250,000 miles per hour, drawn by mutual gravitational attraction. Long-term orbital projections indicate Andromeda is destined to collide with the Milky Way in approximately 4 billion years. Because the distances between individual stars are immense, actual stellar collisions will be rare, but gravitational forces will violently warp both galaxies. Over an additional two billion years, their galactic cores will coalesce, transforming the two magnificent spirals into a single giant elliptical galaxy. This will not be Andromeda's first massive smashup: roughly 2 billion years ago, Andromeda collided with and stripped a massive companion galaxy, leaving behind the compact satellite remnant M32 and a vast stream of stellar debris.
angle: Andromeda is hurtling directly toward the Milky Way at 250,000 miles per hour, destined to collide and merge into a single giant elliptical galaxy.

claims.claim: The Andromeda Galaxy is located approximately 2.5 million light-years from Earth.
Andromeda is the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way.
Edwin Hubble used Cepheid variable stars to establish that Andromeda is an independent galaxy outside the Milky Way.
Andromeda's distance was directly calculated using an eclipsing binary star system made of hot blue O-type and B-type stars.
Andromeda is tilted at an inclination of approximately 77 degrees relative to Earth's line of sight.
Hubble Space Telescope observations were combined into a mosaic of Andromeda assembled from roughly 600 separate fields of view over 10 years.
The Hubble mosaic resolves an estimated 200 million stars in Andromeda that are hotter than our Sun.
Andromeda is moving toward the Milky Way at roughly 250,000 miles per hour (about 110 kilometers per second).
Andromeda and the Milky Way have been predicted to collide in roughly 4 billion years.
The collision between Andromeda and the Milky Way is expected to eventually form a single giant elliptical galaxy.
A major galactic collision occurred at Andromeda approximately 2 billion years ago.
The satellite galaxy M32 is considered to be the stripped core of a galaxy that collided with Andromeda.
Andromeda's Giant Stellar Stream was created by a major past galactic merger.
Both Andromeda and the Milky Way have accreted roughly 100 to 200 low-mass galaxies over the past 12 billion years.
Stars in Andromeda's extended stellar halo are metal-poor.
Stars in Andromeda's visible disk rotate at velocities of around 200 kilometers per second.
Infrared observations revealed that Andromeda contains concentric rings of cold dust and gas where new stars are forming.

disputed: Collision certainty: S2 states Hubble measurements proved a guaranteed head-on collision in 4 billion years, whereas S1 cites newer calculations including Gaia data indicating a roughly 50% probability over 10 billion years (attribute: 'while earlier Hubble models pointed to a guaranteed smashup, newer calculations suggest roughly a 50% chance').

Relative mass: S1 notes Andromeda was historically estimated to be 25% to 50% more massive than the Milky Way, but recent studies suggest equal mass or that the Milky Way is more massive (attribute: 'earlier estimates made Andromeda the heavyweight, but newer studies indicate the Milky Way may be equally or more massive').
